Photograph: Ishika Samant/Getty Images US news LeBron James sues sports betting app Bron for using nickname and likeness without permission
 NBA star’s lawsuit alleges ‘previously unknown app’ acted illegally ‘to gain notoriety’ by seeming affiliated with James
 Agencies Wed 18 Nov 2026 09.03 EST Last modified on Wed 18 Nov 2026 10.05 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google LeBron James sued the sports betting research app Bron on Tuesday, accusing it of trademark infringement for using his nickname ⁠and an artificial intelligence-generated ⁠likeness of him in ​a recent ad campaign without permission.
 In a complaint filed in New York City federal court, the Philadelphia 76ers star, whose nickname is Bron, said he carefully protects his image and chooses who to endorse, reflecting his ⁠status as “one of the most recognizable identities in the world”, and commands tens of millions of dollars for endorsing products or ventures.
 James’s endorsement is “uniquely valuable”, the complaint said. “And that is why defendants decided to ⁠steal it all for themselves.“
 The complaint asks the court to block the makers from using James’s name, to give up any money they have already made and to award damages – including fair market value for the use of his name as well as punitive damages.
 “Defendants did not care that they had engaged in illegal conduct to gain notoriety for their previously unknown app,” the lawsuit states. “They intentionally created the false impression that Mr James endorsed and was affiliated with their Bron App, in an effort to drive downloads and paid subscriptions.”
 ‘It’s sad seeing players promote it’: Wembanyama says he will never endorse gambling companies Read more Bron did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the lawsuit.
 The app’s developer, PlayVision Inc, is based in California. It was launched by the chief executive, Anish Gupta, and chief technology officer, Marc Zoghby, in 2025, with backing from the startup accelerator Y Combinator, as a program that would use artificial intelligence to analyze game and practice footage for sports teams and fans.
 This year, the company released its “Bron” app, which it says does not take direct wagers but charges a subscription fee for services such as bet tracking and odds comparisons. It launched a marketing campaign this month that featured an image of a person resembling James – down to his tattoos, voice and No 23 jersey – sitting in a locker room and scrolling through the app.
 James’s lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter, as previously reported by Front Office Sports . The company took the ad down, but not before it had been reposted and viewed about 1m times, the lawsuit alleged.
 Gupta responded to the attorneys’ demand on social media by writing that the app would get a new name, but no new name had been adopted by the time the lawsuit was filed, leading James’s legal team to suggest the company was milking the controversy for attention. Gupta wrote on social media this week that the new name would be announced on Wednesday.
 The lawsuit notes that James typically commands tens of millions of dollars for such endorsement deals, and that he already has an exclusive deal with the prediction market platform Polymarket . It alleges that the app’s marketing was especially harmful in part because it showed the AI-generated James scrolling through bets involving NBA players.
 “The integrity of NBA competition – and the public’s confidence that players are not betting on the games they play – is of paramount importance to the league, its players, and its fans,” the lawsuit said. “Any suggestion that an active NBA player is betting on NBA games is therefore far from a trivial matter, and it should not be used for clicks and views.”
 James, 41, is the NBA’s all-time leading ‌scorer, with four MVP ‌awards and four league championships. He also has three Olympic gold medals.
